title: Animal Behavior / Ethology
short: What animals actually do in the world: how a behavior develops, what triggers it, and what purpose it serves.
bigPicture: Animal behavior is the scientific study of what animals do and why, covering communication, movement, feeding, mating, social life, learning, and responses to the environment. It has a long-established research literature and its own credential structure for applied practitioners. The field is genuinely interdisciplinary: people enter it from biology, psychology, animal science, wildlife biology, and zoology, and the certification requirements for applied behaviorists recognize all of those routes.

terms.definition: The biological study of animal behavior, especially in natural conditions and with attention to how behavior evolved.
A catalogue of the distinct behaviors a species performs, defined precisely enough that different observers score them the same way.
The study of how behavior contributes to survival and reproduction in a given environment.
Learning in which the consequences of a behavior change how often it occurs; the basis of most modern animal training.
Adding something the animal wants after a behavior, making that behavior more likely to happen again.
Using behavioral science to solve practical problems in training, husbandry, welfare, and problem behavior.
Playing a recorded signal to an animal and measuring the response, used to test what a signal communicates.

focus.title: Mechanism and development
focus.description: What causes a behavior in the moment, and how it emerges over an animal's lifetime through genetics, maturation, experience, and learning.
focus.source: Association for the Study of Animal Behaviour (ASAB): the journal Animal Behaviour

focus.title: Function and evolution
focus.description: What a behavior accomplishes for the animal and how selection shaped it. Behavioral ecology sits here, connecting behavior to survival, reproduction, and environment.
focus.source: Association for the Study of Animal Behaviour (ASAB): the journal Animal Behaviour

focus.title: Social behavior and communication
focus.description: How animals signal, coordinate, compete, cooperate, and organize into groups, and how those systems break down or shift under changed conditions.
focus.source: Association for the Study of Animal Behaviour (ASAB): the journal Animal Behaviour

focus.title: Applied animal behavior
focus.description: Using behavioral science to solve practical problems: training, behavior modification, husbandry, enrichment, handling, and resolving problem behavior in animals under human care.
focus.source: Animal Behavior Society: Applied Animal Behavior

questions.question: Why does this animal do this, and what triggers it?
questions.approach: By building an ethogram, recording behavior systematically against context, and then testing candidate triggers experimentally rather than inferring them from observation alone.

questions.question: How does this behavior develop, and how much of it is learned?
questions.approach: By following individuals from early life, comparing animals with different experience, and running controlled learning tests to separate maturation from experience.

questions.question: What does the behavior accomplish for the animal?
questions.approach: By measuring consequences — feeding success, mating outcomes, survival — and comparing individuals or species that do it more or less.

questions.question: How do these animals communicate?
questions.approach: By recording signals, characterizing their structure, and running playback or presentation experiments to see how receivers respond.

questions.question: Why do individuals of the same species behave differently?
questions.approach: By repeated testing of the same individuals across contexts to see whether differences are consistent, then relating them to sex, age, condition, or history.

questions.question: How can behavioral knowledge improve care, training, or management?
questions.approach: By defining the target behavior in observable terms, applying learning principles in a structured plan, and measuring whether the behavior actually changed.

responsibilities: Design observation protocols and collect systematic behavioral data.
Analyze behavioral data and test hypotheses about cause or function.
Apply behavioral principles to training, enrichment, handling, or problem behavior.
Advise caretakers, owners, or managers and document outcomes.

variations.label: Research versus applied
variations.description: Research behavior work asks why animals do what they do; applied behavior work uses that knowledge to change outcomes for specific animals. The Animal Behavior Society certifies applied practitioners at two levels, requiring graduate-level behavioral coursework plus at least two years of professional experience.
variations.source: Animal Behavior Society (ABS): Certified Applied Animal Behaviorist requirements

variations.label: Entry disciplines
variations.description: Behaviorists come out of animal science, ethology, psychology, wildlife biology, behavioral ecology, and zoology. There is no single required major, which is unusual in this space.
variations.source: Animal Behavior Society (ABS): Certified Applied Animal Behaviorist requirements

variations.label: Setting
variations.description: The same science supports work in laboratories, zoos, farms, shelters, universities, and private consulting.

variations.label: Species
variations.description: Wild, farm, companion, and laboratory animals all have behavior specialists, and the applied literature is largely organized by that split.

realities: Applied certification requires graduate coursework and documented professional experience, not just interest or hands-on hours.
Behavior work is observation-heavy and often slow; data collection can take far longer than analysis.
Many applied roles are self-employed or consulting rather than salaried positions.
The title 'animal behaviorist' is not legally protected, so credentials matter for credibility.
